topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A process has its own execution context and resource relationships. Starting one is not the same as calling a function in another thread. This chapter launches a controlled child image with posix_spawn, passes a minimal explicit environment, and interprets its exit status. The child is the same executable in a separate mode, so the test does not depend on a shell command string or interpolate untrusted text.

blocks.text: A maintenance tool launches another executable and sees a zero return from the launch function. It reports success before the child has read its configuration. Seconds later the child exits with an error, leaving the operator with a misleading success message and no recorded exit status. Starting work and completing work are different events, even when the interface makes launch look like a single operation.

blocks.text: Process management adds identity, inherited resources, environment, executable selection, and reaping to the lifetime reasoning developed for ordinary C++ objects. The parent and child do not share the same control flow after an image replacement. A parent must decide which failures it reports immediately, which results require waiting, and how the child is stopped and collected when the surrounding operation fails.

topics.title: 12.1.1 Creating Child Processes
topics.summary: POSIX systems provide several process-creation mechanisms. fork creates a child with a related copy of the parent’s process state, while spawn interfaces combine creation with launching a selected program under specified file and attribute actions. The choice affects inherited resources, failure handling, and what code can safely run in the child before a new image is installed.

blocks.text: A process is an operating-system execution context with an address space, threads, credentials, open resources, and other state. Linux fork creates a child process whose initial memory reflects the parent, but the two normally evolve in separate address spaces. Implementation techniques such as copy-on-write can avoid immediately copying every page; they do not make ordinary heap variables into a synchronized cross-process communication channel. (FORK)

blocks.text: Forking a multithreaded process adds a serious restriction. Only the calling thread exists in the child, while inherited memory can reflect locks held by threads that no longer exist there. Calling ordinary allocation, C++ stream, or mutex code in that state can deadlock or violate the required post-fork constraints. Between fork and successful exec in such a child, use only operations permitted by the relevant async-signal-safety rules. A normal-looking helper can call unsafe code internally. (SIGNALSAFE)

It takes an executable path, argument and environment vectors, and optional file actions and attributes. It still requires deliberate choices about inherited state; it is not a sandbox or a substitute for validating which program is being launched. The worked example uses a fixed program and a small explicit environment.

blocks.text: The parent owns a lifecycle responsibility, not merely a numeric PID. If an exception occurs after successful creation, the program must still arrange the required waiting or termination. A child can remain running after the parent abandons its local variable. Design a process owner or supervisory scope whose cleanup policy is documented; do not assume that a C++ destructor for a PID integer has any operating-system effect.

topics.title: 12.1.2 Replacing Process Images
topics.summary: An exec-family operation replaces the current process image with a new program on success; it does not return to the old code as an ordinary successful function call. The process identity and selected resource relationships follow platform rules, while the address space and program state are replaced. A failed exec returns an error to the old image.

blocks.text: An exec-family operation replaces the current process image with another program when it succeeds. It does not create an additional process by itself. The successful call does not return to the old program’s next statement, because that program image has been replaced. Failure returns an error within the still-existing old image, and the child must take an explicit failure path rather than accidentally continuing parent logic.

blocks.text: Arguments are a vector of strings terminated by a null pointer, not one shell command line. Spaces inside an argument remain part of that argument. Shell expansion, pipelines, wildcard processing, and redirection do not occur merely because a string contains shell punctuation. Keeping arguments separate avoids a large class of quoting and injection errors, but the invoked program still interprets its own options and operands.

blocks.text: Executable selection needs a trust boundary. An explicit reviewed path avoids accidentally selecting a same-named program from an untrusted search directory. Search-based variants follow a path policy that must be understood. Do not construct a privileged launch by concatenating uncontrolled input into a shell command. Prefer a fixed executable and a validated argument vector, with -- where that particular tool supports an end-of-options marker.

blocks.text: Open descriptors survive image replacement unless close-on-exec or explicit file actions remove them. An inherited listening socket, temporary file, or secret-bearing pipe can keep resources alive or expand the child’s capabilities. Inventory what the new program needs and pass only those resources deliberately. The acquisition-time close-on-exec policies from earlier chapters help make default inheritance narrower.

topics.title: 12.2.1 Passing Environment Information
topics.summary: A process environment is a collection of name-value strings made available to the new program. Passing an explicit environment can avoid inheriting unrelated secrets, locale settings, or library-control variables. It also means the child does not automatically receive PATH or other settings it might need, so use a known executable path and document required variables.

blocks.text: Avoid modifying a shared process environment as a way to configure one child while other threads may read or launch against it. Similarly, a child working directory should be specified through a controlled mechanism rather than racing a global chdir in a multithreaded parent.

topics.title: 12.2.2 Handling Exit Status
topics.summary: Waiting for a child reports a status value whose fields must be interpreted with platform macros. A child that has finished but has not been reaped can remain as a zombie entry until the parent collects its status.

A child that has finished but has not been reaped can remain as a zombie entry until the parent collects its status.

blocks.text: First ask whether the child exited normally. Only then interpret its normal exit status. A child terminated by a signal has a different outcome, and attempting to describe it as an ordinary application error number loses information. Logs should distinguish launch failure, normal nonzero exit, signal termination, wait failure, and timeout or cancellation initiated by the supervisor.

blocks.text: The example deliberately has its child exit with seven. The parent considers that the expected fixture outcome, not a general success convention for all programs. Most command-line programs conventionally use zero for success, but each tool’s documented interface defines the meaning of other values. Keep the expected status in the test contract rather than assuming every nonzero status represents the same kind of defect.

blocks.text: A child that has terminated still needs to be reaped according to the operating system’s process model. Abandoning repeated child results can accumulate zombie entries and lose operational evidence. Conversely, waiting forever for a child whose input can stall is not an acceptable complete supervisor design. A deadline requires a policy for observing progress, requesting termination, escalating when necessary, and collecting the final status.

blocks.text: Termination is not rollback. The child may already have written files, sent requests, or acquired external resources. A supervisor should record what was attempted and what remains uncertain after forced termination. A robust job protocol can use transaction identifiers, staged outputs, or explicit completion markers to make recovery possible. Do not describe kill followed by waitpid as proof that no partial work happened.

topics.title: Failure clinic — The child that survived the error path
topics.summary: Suppose a parent launches a child, then fails to create its logging file. It throws before calling wait. The child can continue working, while the operator sees only the parent’s logging error. Repair the lifecycle ownership so every successful launch enters a supervisory scope immediately. That scope must decide whether to wait, request termination, or transfer responsibility to another owner.

Two concurrent launches overwrite the same variable and receive each other’s settings. An explicit environment vector removes that coupling without requiring a global lock around unrelated work.

blocks.text: Finally, a child uses C++ streams and heap allocation after fork in a multithreaded parent and hangs before exec. Use a launch design that avoids unsafe child-side work, or reduce that branch to the permitted operations required to enter the new image.

Write a design for a timed child supervisor without immediately implementing signal escalation. Specify the deadline origin, how the parent waits without losing the ability to enforce it, what constitutes graceful termination, what happens after a grace period, and who performs the final wait. State what partial external effects remain possible.

For inheritance review, list every descriptor the parent owns at launch. Classify each as deliberately passed, close-on-exec, or accidentally inherited. A program that cannot explain its child descriptor set is not ready to launch untrusted or privileged work. Keep the exercise within owned test resources.

Review reasoning. Does exec create a second process? Not by itself. Does successful spawn prove the child’s task succeeded? No. Is a wait status directly the exit code? No. Can a parent exception automatically terminate its child? Not without an explicit owner or supervisor policy. Why avoid global environment changes? They turn local launch configuration into shared mutable process state.

Completion criterion. Deliver a launch configuration object, a result type that preserves outcome categories, and tests for expected and failed launches. The parent must have an explicit owner for each child from creation through reaping, including the paths where the parent’s own work fails.
